title: Phase distinction of Gibbs states without symmetry breaking: topological invariants of the 3D toric code
abstract: We study the finite-temperature topological order of the three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code in a generic magnetic field, where every higher-form symmetry is explicitly broken and can at most be emergent. We show perturbatively, and confirm by large-scale quantum Monte Carlo, that the topological entanglement entropy stays quantized at $γ= \ln 2$ throughout the topological phase -- at finite temperature and under the symmetry-breaking field alike -- and collapses to $0$ across the thermal transition, a quantization protected geometrically by the Bianchi identity rather than by any exact symmetry of the system. The plateau $γ= \ln 2$ is, however, not invariant under quasi-local channels: a constant-depth channel can generate this identical quantized value from a trivial product state. We therefore introduce the decoded Wilson-loop correlation $f_W$, which quantizes to $1$ in the topological phase and $0$ in the trivial phase as $L\to\infty$ and, unlike $γ$, is a quasi-local-channel invariant -- a robust topological invariant of the mixed state.
summary: This research tackles the challenge of identifying robust topological phase transitions at non-zero temperatures without relying on symmetry breaking. By introducing the decoded Wilson-loop correlation $f_W$, the authors provide a new, quasi-local-channel invariant diagnostic that successfully maps out the full phase diagram of the 3D toric code. This work advances our understanding of how topological order persists and manifests in realistic, thermal quantum systems.
main_problem: The central problem is establishing robust topological invariants that can distinguish between different phases of matter at non-zero temperature ($T>0$) without relying on the spontaneous breaking of any exact symmetry.
main_result: The decoded Wilson-loop correlation $f_W$ was introduced as a quasi-local-channel invariant order parameter, which successfully distinguishes topological (value 1) from trivial (value 0) phases across finite temperatures and external fields.
method: The study employs theoretical analysis combined with large-scale Quantum Monte Carlo simulations to probe the thermal Gibbs state ($ho_ eta$) of the system.
model_or_system: The primary model is the three-dimensional ($	ext{3D}$) $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code, analyzed in its finite-temperature Gibbs state under generic magnetic fields where higher-form symmetries are explicitly broken or emergent.
key_observables: Topological Entanglement Entropy ($\gamma$), Decoded Wilson-loop correlation ($f_W$), and various string/loop correlators (e.g., $\langle  ar{W}_1  ar{W}_2 angle$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), external magnetic fields $(h_x, h_z)$, and system size ($L$). The critical temperature $T_c$ is often compared to the 3D Ising model transition point.
main_assumptions: The rigorous definition of phase equivalence for Gibbs states at $T>0$ remains an active area of research; some results rely on quasi-local channel invariance arguments.
figures_summary: Figures compare various diagnostics ($\gamma$, $ho_{FM}$, correlators) across T-scans, $h_x$-scans, and $h_z$-scans, showing how different observables are sensitive to different types of phase transitions (thermal vs. magnetic vs. electric).
paper_structure: The paper develops by first identifying the failure points of conventional diagnostics ($\gamma$ is not channel invariant), then introducing robust invariants like $f_W$, and finally applying these tools across the full $(h_x, h_z, T)$ phase diagram to demonstrate a universal diagnostic.
why_interesting: The work provides advanced techniques for characterizing topological order in thermal equilibrium states, which is crucial for understanding quantum materials where finite temperature effects are dominant. The focus on channel-invariant diagnostics is highly relevant to open quantum systems theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The three tiers of states and their phase-equivalence relations. Pure gapped ground states (bottom) are classified by finite-depth local unitaries—equivalently, quasi-adiabatic continuation along a path of local Hamiltonians with no gap closing [15, 16]. General mixed states (top) are classified by two-way quasi-local channels [17–19]. The intermediate Gibbs tier is classified by a path of local Hamiltonians with no ther- modynamic singularity.
